title: Derive the MOSFET I–V law and identify where it breaks
summary: Develop the gradual-channel model from inversion charge, obtain triode/saturation and transconductance, then test short-channel and body-bias limits.
objectives: Derive I–V by integrating inversion charge rather than memorizing it.
Compute saturation boundaries and bias headroom.
Extract gm, gm/ID and a first-order output resistance.
Explain body effect, DIBL and velocity saturation as distinct phenomena.

sections.title: 1. Prerequisites: the MOS electrostatic boundary
sections.html:
An ideal enhancement NMOS is formed in p-type silicon under a gate dielectric. A positive gate-to-source bias changes the electrostatic surface potential; beyond a threshold approximation it supports an electron inversion channel. The threshold is not a universal material constant: it responds to substrate doping, oxide thickness, gate work function, trapped charge, body bias, temperature, channel geometry and drain-induced barrier lowering.

In an ideal strong-inversion charge-sheet model, with source at \(V_S=0\) and local channel potential \(V(x)\), the magnitude of mobile inversion charge per area is approximately \(|Q_i(x)|=C'_{ox}[V_{GS}-V_T-V(x)]\). We assume constant mobility, negligible depletion-charge variation along the channel, a long device, a gradual electric field and charge near the Si–oxide interface. The bracket must remain nonnegative wherever the charge-sheet approximation is used.

sections.title: 2. Relate channel charge to current
sections.html:
A slice of inversion channel has mobile charge per unit length \(W|Q_i(x)|\). Under the local drift approximation, its current is \(I_D=\mu_n W|Q_i(x)|\,\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}x\). This is a conventional drain-current magnitude with \(V\) increasing from source to drain.

Substitute the charge relation, define overdrive \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T\), multiply by \(\mathrm{d}x\), and integrate from source to drain: \(I_D\int_0^L\mathrm{d}x=\mu_n WC'_{ox}\int_0^{V_{DS}}(V_{OV}-V)\,\mathrm{d}V\). Evaluating the integral gives \(I_D=(\mu_n C'_{ox}W/L)[V_{OV}V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2/2]\), the ideal triode/linear-region law.

Check units: \(\mu_n C'_{ox}(W/L)\) has units A/V². Multiplying by volts squared gives amperes. Do this check before typing a number; confusing \(C'_{ox}\) per unit area with device-total capacitance breaks the derivation.

sections.title: 3. Why the long-channel current saturates
sections.html:
At the drain end \(x=L\), charge-sheet inversion approaches zero when \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\). Substituting the boundary into the triode expression yields \(I_{D,sat}=\tfrac12\mu_n C'_{ox}(W/L)V_{OV}^2\). Beyond this ideal boundary, the extra drain bias drops mainly across a near-drain high-field region; the simplest long-channel model treats the terminal current as constant.

**Saturation here does not mean unlimited voltage tolerance or absolute current independence.** Channel-length modulation increases drain current with \(V_{DS}\), and velocity saturation changes scaling for short channels. The square-law derivation only controls a limited operating regime. Its actual use is to understand bias trends, not to predict modern nanometer-CMOS signoff accuracy.

sections.title: 4. Differential parameters: gm, gds and intrinsic gain
sections.html:
For the ideal saturation expression, \(g_m=(\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS})_{V_{DS}}=\mu_n C'_{ox}(W/L)V_{OV}=2I_D/V_{OV}\). Thus \(g_m/I_D=2/V_{OV}\) in strong-inversion square-law conditions. It is a useful first-order efficiency measure: high transconductance for a given bias current can help analog gain, but bandwidth, noise, inversion level and matching impose competing constraints.

A first-order channel-length modulation model uses \(I_D\approx I_{D0}(1+\lambda V_{DS})\). Locally \(g_{ds}\approx\lambda I_{D0}\), so \(r_o\approx1/(\lambda I_D)\) when \(\lambda V_{DS}\) is small and the approximation is consistently applied. Intrinsic small-signal voltage gain magnitude is roughly \(g_mr_o\); it declines as finite output conductance grows.

sections.title: 5. Body bias and the depletion region
sections.html:
For an NMOS in a p-type body, increasing reverse source-to-body voltage \(V_{SB}>0\) generally expands depletion charge and increases threshold. The classical expression is \(V_T(V_{SB})=V_{T0}+\gamma[\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}]\). Here \(2\phi_F\) is a positive magnitude in that convention. The body-effect coefficient \(\gamma\) depends on semiconductor and oxide parameters.

A source-follower whose source rises can therefore experience both reduced \(V_{GS}\) and increased \(V_T\). These are separate effects. Some modern devices have heavily engineered bodies or alternative structures; apply the model only when its premises are valid.

sections.title: 6. Scaling breaks assumptions in several different ways
sections.html:
Shorter channels experience strong lateral fields. Carrier speed ceases to increase linearly with field (velocity saturation), drain electric field lowers the source-channel barrier (DIBL), and junction electrostatics encroach into the channel (short-channel rolloff). Gate leakage, subthreshold current, quantum effects and parasitic resistances can also matter. A model that fits one I–V curve does not uniquely identify which mechanism is responsible.

An effective simulator comparison varies one physical mechanism at a time and reports its effect on threshold, subthreshold slope, output current and temperature behavior. Device width, finger geometry and layout parasitics must be treated explicitly when moving from a transistor model to a real amplifier.

sections.title: 7. From physical theory to circuit design
sections.html:
To design a common-source or differential-stage bias, first choose power/current and available supply swing. Obtain realistic transistor curves or PDK models; calculate \(g_m\), \(g_{ds}\), and capacitances around the actual operating point. Only then decide the gain, speed and noise budget. Use hand calculations to detect a mistaken bias, and simulator corner checks to explore process and temperature variability.

Do not present a hand-derived square-law current as a foundry simulation result. In reports, label analytical estimate, compact-model prediction, TCAD prediction and measurement separately.

sections.title: Why threshold is not an ideal on/off switch
sections.html:
On a physical transistor, current does not suddenly appear at one exact gate voltage. Even below the commonly extracted threshold, thermally activated diffusion can move carriers along the surface. In a useful simplified weak-inversion regime, current varies approximately exponentially with gate bias, whereas the strong-inversion charge-sheet model leads to an approximate square law. Both approximate regimes describe the *same physical device* and meet through moderate inversion.

In weak inversion, a commonly used local approximation is \(I_D\propto \exp[(V_{GS}-V_T)/(nV_{\mathrm{th}})]\) with subthreshold slope factor \(n>1\). Differentiate its logarithm: \(g_m/I_D\approx 1/(nV_{\mathrm{th}})\). At 300 K with \(n=1.5\), this is roughly \(25.8\,\mathrm{V}^{-1}\), compared with \(10\,\mathrm{V}^{-1}\) for a square-law device at \(V_{OV}=0.20\,\mathrm V\). This does *not* mean weak inversion always produces the best amplifier: it often involves less current density and lower speed for a fixed device area.

The MOS threshold should be associated with a clearly stated extraction convention. Some technologies report constant-current threshold, others extract from linear-current extrapolation or mathematical compact-model parameters. Comparing two unlabeled threshold numbers can be misleading, especially when geometry, drain bias and measurement temperature differ.

sections.title: A practical gm/ID decision tree
sections.html:
Analog design starts with desired noise, gain, bandwidth, power and output swing. A traditional overdrive approach sizes transistor width by solving the long-channel current law for W/L. A gm/ID approach instead chooses an inversion level and uses a device-specific relationship between current efficiency, intrinsic gain, capacitances and current density. In a real technology, those relationships come from measured or compact-model-generated lookup tables.

Suppose a target current is \(I_D=100\,\mu\mathrm A\) and an ideal strong-inversion overdrive is \(V_{OV}=0.20\,\mathrm V\). Then \(g_m=2I_D/V_{OV}=1\,\mathrm{mS}\). If the process gives \(\mu C'_{ox}=100\,\mu\mathrm{A/V^2}\), solving the ideal saturation law gives \(W/L=2I_D/(\mu C'_{ox}V_{OV}^2)=50\). This is a first sizing estimate, not a foundry-calibrated layout result.

Why must we revisit the estimate? Wider transistors create larger gate/diffusion capacitances, and a drain current budget sets both thermal-noise and power tradeoffs. Designers compare gm, gm/ID, gm/gds, fT and capacitances at the actual bias point and across process/voltage/temperature (PVT) corners. The best choice differs for an always-on low-noise sensor frontend and a high-speed ADC driver.

sections.title: Extract gm and output conductance from I–V sweeps
sections.html:
Derivatives are experimentally useful local measurements. Once an ID–VGS or ID–VDS dataset is available, estimate gm with a centered difference at fixed VDS and output conductance gds with a centered difference at fixed VGS. Choose voltage perturbations small enough to approximate derivatives, but not so small that numerical or instrument noise dominates. Smoothness, bias state and model region matter.

The numerical formulas are \(g_m\approx[I_D(V_{GS}+h,V_{DS})-I_D(V_{GS}-h,V_{DS})]/(2h)\) and \(g_{ds}\approx[I_D(V_{GS},V_{DS}+h)-I_D(V_{GS},V_{DS}-h)]/(2h)\). In a consistent positive-current convention, both are in siemens. Then \(r_o=1/g_{ds}\) for nonzero positive output conductance. If a simulator produces source-oriented current, check its sign definition before differentiating.

Do not take gm directly from one current measurement or infer output resistance from an I–V plot whose horizontal scale is unknown. For serious work, show the sweep interval, extracted bias point, units, derivative step size and a sensitivity check showing gm does not change dramatically when h is halved.

sections.title: A complete first-pass common-source design
sections.html:
Imagine an analog supply of 1.8 V. You want a low-power transistor stage with drain current of 100 µA and overdrive around 0.2 V in a simplified long-channel model. If the drain resistor is 5 kΩ, its DC voltage drop is 0.5 V, leaving drain DC potential near 1.3 V. The device is in the *ideal* saturation region if its VDS exceeds VOV (assuming its source is at 0 V). This verifies the operating *point*, not the entire output swing.

At \(g_m=1\,\mathrm{mS}\), if \(r_o=125\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\) and the next-stage load is \(R_L=10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\), the midband small-signal gain estimate is \(A_v=-g_m(R_D\parallel r_o\parallel R_L)\approx -3.20\ \mathrm{V/V}\). Remove the load and the gain changes. Add source degeneration and the gain changes again. The circuit may distort or clip if the input excursion drives the transistor outside the range where the local derivative is valid.

Real designers must also calculate amplifier input/output capacitances, thermal and flicker noise, common-mode limits, load requirements, startup bias stability, supply rejection and layout-related mismatch. A successful DC bias is the *first check* of a working circuit, not the last.

sections.title: Hands-on: reproduce a transistor current sweep in SPICE
sections.html:
Start with the ideal model so you know what the simulator *should* produce. This example uses a deliberately simple Level-1 NMOS compact model in ngspice. The model parameter KP corresponds to the chosen process transconductance parameter in the idealized LEVEL=1 interpretation; W and L choose geometry. Verify your simulator's MOS model syntax in its installed documentation.

* Educational Level-1 NMOS current sweep
Vg g 0 DC 0.85
Vd d 0 DC 0
M1 d g 0 0 nmos_ideal W=50u L=1u
.model nmos_ideal NMOS (LEVEL=1 VTO=0.45 KP=100u LAMBDA=0.0)
.dc Vd 0 1.5 0.025
.control
run
plot -i(Vd)
.endc
.end

Save as a SPICE netlist and run it in an environment with ngspice installed. For VGS = 0.85 V and VT = 0.45 V, overdrive is 0.40 V; ideal β is 5 mA/V² and saturation current should approach about 0.40 mA once VDS exceeds about 0.40 V. Note that ngspice reports the current through an independent voltage source with a source-oriented sign; plotting −i(Vd) often makes the drain-current direction positive. This example has not been run inside this website.

Then run four investigations separately: halve VGS overdrive, change W/L, enable a nonzero LAMBDA, and change the load. Save each curve and explain *why* it moves. Finally find an open PDK compatible with your simulator and repeat using its compact models, clearly marking differences caused by the more realistic device description.

example.title: From overdrive to gain efficiency and output resistance
example.problem: An illustrative long-channel NMOS has β = μn C′ox(W/L)=200 µA/V², VOV=0.20 V and an independent local channel-length-modulation parameter λ=0.08 V⁻¹. Estimate nominal saturated current and ideal gm from the square-law part, then a first-order ro at this current. State why the numbers are only approximate.
steps: The \(g_m\) and \(r_o\) estimates combine simple approximations; for a consistent finite-\(\lambda\) operating point, account for the chosen \(V_{DS}\) and extract both derivatives from the same local current model or simulated I–V data.

checks.prompt: Derive the triode-region I–V law by integrating a linearly decreasing inversion charge.
checks.hint: Write (|Q_i(x)|=C'_{ox}(V_{OV}-V)), then integrate (I_D dx=mu W|Q_i|dV) along the channel.

checks.prompt: For VGS=1.1 V and VT=0.45 V, what VDS marks the ideal long-channel saturation boundary?
checks.answer: \(V_{OV}=1.1-0.45=0.65\ \mathrm{V}\). Ideal long-channel saturation starts at about \(V_{DS}\ge0.65\ \mathrm{V}\), within model assumptions.

checks.prompt: With β=1 mA/V² and VOV=0.3 V, calculate ID,sat and gm.
A stage has gm=2 mS, ro=50 kΩ and RD=10 kΩ. Estimate gain ignoring other loads.
checks.hint: For AC-grounded supply and fixed source, (A_vapprox-g_m(R_Dparallel r_o)).

checks.prompt: Two NMOS devices have the same W/L, but one has a much shorter L. Must their measured ID–VG curves match?
checks.hint: What effects violate a simple long-channel W/L law?
checks.answer: No. Velocity saturation, DIBL, channel-length modulation, source/drain series resistance, mobility degradation and geometry-dependent threshold can alter current even at identical \(W/L\).

checks.prompt: If a circuit designer maximizes gm/ID without considering capacitance, does bandwidth automatically increase?
checks.answer: No. Bandwidth depends on \(g_m/C\), poles, parasitic loading and bias. A transistor can have favorable \(g_m/I_D\) while increased area and capacitance harm speed.

checks.prompt: For γ=0.4 V^0.5, 2φF=0.6 V, and VSB=0.4 V, estimate ΔVT.
checks.answer: \(\Delta V_T=0.4(\sqrt{1.0}-\sqrt{0.6})\approx0.4(1-0.77460)\approx0.0902\ \mathrm{V}\). This is a classical square-root estimate.

checks.prompt: An engineer says that an NMOS carries exactly zero drain current when VGS is 10 mV below threshold. Explain why this statement is physically inaccurate.
checks.hint: Recall the gradual transition through weak inversion and the limitations of the square-law cutoff approximation.
checks.answer: Subthreshold conduction usually exists because carriers can diffuse even below the threshold extracted by a chosen convention. A simplified weak-inversion model has \(I_D\propto\exp[(V_{GS}-V_T)/(nV_{\mathrm{th}})]\), not a perfect discontinuous switch. Whether the current matters depends on device and application.

checks.prompt: For ID=100 µA, μC′ox=100 µA/V² and VOV=0.2 V, calculate the ideal W/L needed in saturation, plus gm.
checks.answer: \(W/L=2(100\,\mu A)/[(100\,\mu A/V^2)(0.20\,V)^2]=50\). \(g_m=2I_D/V_{OV}=1\,\mathrm{mS}\). This is an ideal first sizing only.

checks.prompt: A measured output-characteristic sweep gives 100 µA at 0.9 V and 104 µA at 1.1 V, for fixed gate bias. Estimate gds and ro using a secant approximation.
checks.hint: Use ΔID / ΔVDS. Convert microamperes to amperes.
checks.answer: \(g_{ds}\approx(104-100)\,\mu A/(1.1-0.9)\,V=20\,\mu S\). Hence \(r_o\approx1/(20\,\mu S)=50\,k\Omega\). This estimate covers a finite interval, not an infinitesimal derivative.

checks.prompt: Your level-1 SPICE curve predicts 0.4 mA at VGS=0.85 V, but your BSIM PDK model predicts 0.25 mA. Does this prove the PDK is wrong?
checks.hint: Which physical and compact-model effects were omitted from the simple model?
checks.answer: No. Mobility reduction, series resistance, threshold shifts, short-channel effects and calibrated process parameters differ. Verify model/device geometry, voltage and temperature definitions, then compare to measured silicon or reliable PDK characterization.

capstone.title: Characterize and design an NMOS bias point from scratch
capstone.brief: Compare a hand-derived long-channel model with simulated I–V families; quantify how model nonidealities change a useful analog bias decision.
deliverables: A Python model producing labelled ID–VDS families for at least five overdrives, with the triode/saturation boundaries shown.
A voltage-bias table for three chosen operating points listing ID, VOV, gm, gm/ID and theoretical gain when a load is specified.
An ngspice or equivalent comparison using a documented LEVEL=1 illustrative model, then one realistic compact-model example if a lawful PDK is available.
A 5–8 page comparison discussing region selection, power, output swing, process/temperature caveats and what cannot be inferred without measured data.
acceptance: Every I–V curve is continuous at VDS=VOV and the saturation-boundary prediction is demonstrated analytically.
A numerical finite-difference gm estimate agrees with the ideal analytic derivative within stated tolerance for a sufficiently small voltage increment.
Units for β, gm, current, power and voltage are consistent.
The model is identified as ideal or simulated; no fabricated silicon measurements are claimed.
